title: When the Glasshouse Turns
premise: Quentin Vasquez, once the conservatory's celebrated piano prodigy, returns a decade after her public breakdown to work as a janitor, hiding in plain sight among the people who watched her fall. There she meets Mirela Ondu, the elderly last speaker of Vessari, a dying language, who asks Quentin to become her final student—not to save the language, but so that someone will know how to say goodbye in it. As Mirela's health fails and the conservatory threatens to demolish the old glasshouse where they meet, Quentin must choose between remaining invisible and speaking publicly about what was taken from her and from Mirela. In the end, she performs one last time in the glasshouse, reciting Mirela's farewell in Vessari before an audience of strangers, letting the language die out loud rather than in silence—and claiming her own name for the first time since she lost it.
about_author: Yara Brightwater is the pen name of a former conservatory archivist who spent years cataloguing recordings of endangered languages. She writes literary fiction about the quiet inheritances we refuse and the ones we cannot put down.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. She begins work as a night janitor at the conservatory that once made her famous, moving through its halls like a ghost, avoiding the practice rooms and the portraits of former students—including her own. The emotional beat is numbness disguised as peace; she has mistaken invisibility for safety.

chapters.title: A Woman Who Counts in Threes
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Cleaning the old glasshouse annex, she finds Mirela Ondu, a retired linguist who still holds a key, counting seeds aloud in a language Quentin doesn't recognize. Their first conversation is wary but electric. The beat: curiosity cracking through Quentin's deliberate flatness.

chapters.title: What the Conservatory Keeps
chapters.summary: Mirela's POV. We learn Mirela's history: born to Vessari parents, recorded by academics, outlived every other speaker. She has watched institutions preserve languages like specimens while letting speakers die unvisited. The beat: quiet grief and a decision forming—she wants a student, not an archive.

chapters.title: Lessons Begin
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Mirela asks Quentin to learn Vessari, and Quentin refuses, then returns the next night anyway. First lessons: sounds, names, the word for 'again.' Practicing a new language feels dangerously like practicing music. The beat: terror and hunger arriving together.

chapters.title: The Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. A posted notice announces the glasshouse annex will be demolished for a new recital hall. Mirela shrugs; Quentin rages on her behalf, surprising herself. Meanwhile a former classmate, now a dean, recognizes Quentin. The beat: the past closing in from both directions.

chapters.title: Hands That Remember
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Forced to play for a staff event, Quentin's hands betray her—the muscle memory intact, the panic immediate. She flees to the glasshouse, where Mirela teaches her the Vessari word for 'broken' and insists it is not an insult. The beat: shame met with unexpected tenderness.

chapters.title: Found People
chapters.summary: Mirela's POV. Mirela reflects on the family she never had and recognizes one forming: Quentin, plus a young security guard named Dev who starts sitting in on lessons. But her health declines sharply, and she hides it. The beat: joy shadowed by urgency; found family named at last.

chapters.title: The Word for Goodbye
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Mirela is hospitalized and reveals there is no single Vessari word for goodbye—farewells are spoken differently depending on whether you expect to return. She asks Quentin to give her the kind said when you don't. Quentin realizes this means learning to be witnessed. The beat: dread transfigured into purpose.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, climax. At the public hearing on the demolition, Quentin stands before the deans and donors who remember her fall and speaks—in English first, confessing what the conservatory did to her, then in Vessari, delivering Mirela's formal farewell to the world. The glasshouse is spared pending review; more importantly, Quentin is no longer hiding. The beat: exposure as liberation.

chapters.title: After the Last Speaker
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, resolution. Mirela dies in early spring; Quentin and Dev sit with her, and Quentin speaks the returning-kind of farewell anyway—a promise. She takes a job teaching music to children in the conservatory's outreach program, keeps the glasshouse key, and speaks Vessari aloud to no one, which is no longer no one. The beat: grief carried openly, identity claimed, inheritance accepted.
